lesson_title: Ropes Only Pull: Why Every Muscle Needs a Partner
hook_text: Try to push something with a rope. You can't. Neither can a muscle, and that one fact explains your whole body.
clip_script: Your skeleton is scaffolding: 206 poles. It holds you up, protects your brain and heart, makes blood in the marrow and stores calcium. Your muscles are ropes tied to the poles by tendons. And here is the thing about a rope: it can only pull. Pull your forearm up with the rope on the front, the biceps. Now how do you get it back down? Not by pushing. You need a second rope on the back, the triceps. One pulls, the other goes slack. Every joint that moves has a pair like this: antagonistic pairs. Where two poles meet is a joint, and the type tells you the movement. Elbow and knee: door hinges, one way and back. Shoulder and hip: a ball in a cup, like a gear lever, any direction. The top of your neck: a pivot, like a key in a lock, for shaking your head. Smooth cartilage caps the bones, synovial fluid oils the joint, ligaments strap bone to bone. Tendon, muscle to bone. Ligament, bone to bone. Feed the frame now, calcium, sunshine, exercise, and it will not crumble at seventy.
visual_style: Steel scaffolding morphs into a skeleton; ropes appear along an arm and tug it up and down in turn; a door hinge, a gear lever and a key in a lock snap onto elbow, shoulder and neck.
pacing: A quick frame tour, a slow beat on 'a rope can only pull', three fast joint beats, a one-line finish on bone health.
call_to_action: Watch the full lesson and give the four-part answer for any movement.
